newsitem.title: CHINA: Foreign investment in China to drop-economists.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment in China to drop-economists.

text.p: Foreign investment in China will slip in 1997 and fall more sharply in subsequent years, partly because of the abolition of duty-free imports of capital equipment, Chinese economists said on Tuesday.
Actual foreign investment is expected to decline to around $40 billion this year from a record $42.35 billion in 1996, and then hover at around $30 billion a year between 1998 and 2000, they said.

"This year, it'll be $40 billion...next year, $30 billion could be very difficult," said Ma Yu, director of the department of foreign capital utilisation at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.
But Ma noted that annual actual foreign investment in China -- the world's biggest potential market with a population of 1.2 billion -- would not fall below $25.0 billion.
Low costs for land and labour make China a natural magnet for foreign investment.

China opened its doors to foreign money in the 1970's and in recent years actual foreign investment has soared dramatically from just $4.37 billion in 1991, according to figures provided by the academy.

The figures show that contracted foreign investment, or pledges by foreign businessmen to invest in China, fell to $73.21 billion in 1996 from $91.28 billion in 1995 and a record $111.44 billion in 1993.
Economists attribute the forecast falls in foreign investment in part to China's abolition of duty-free treatment for imports of capital equipment for foreign-invested firms from the end of 1997.
A cooling of double-digit economic growth in recent years to a single-digit pace was also to blame for the shrinking trend, Ma said.
China's economy grew by 9.7 percent last year compared with 10.2 percent in 1995 and 14.2 percent in 1992.
Officials have set a target of eight percent for 1997, although some government economists say the rate could exceed 10.0 percent

A senior government economist who asked not to be identified said China's decision to cut interest rates twice last year coupled with an end to inflation-linked interest rate subsidies on bank deposits had turned away speculative foreign funds.
Ma said China would restrict preferential treatment for foreign investment to specified sectors in future, but declined to identify them.
China is eager for more foreign investment in agriculture as well as the power industry and basic infrastructure projects, including highways, official media have said.

The country is also mulling preferential measures to attract foreign investors to its backward hinterland -- central and western regions whose economic growth and foreign investment lag far behind their booming cousins in eastern coastal areas.
About 80 percent of foreign investment is concentrated in China's coastal provinces.
Accumulated actual foreign investment in China was $177.2 billion at the end of 1996, according to the academy, which is under the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation.
Hong Kong is China's biggest single foreign investor, accounting for more than 60 percent of total overseas investment, followed by the United States and Taiwan.
The senior government economist said China was becoming more selective about foreign investment.

"It may not be pleasing to the ear. We hope for big corporations to come. The smaller ones, we don't care a lot," he said. "We are not very interested... in foreign investment in labour-intensive industries."
State media have said China is considering restrictions on foreign investment in textiles, garments and in sectors where domestic production capacity is already in surplus.
Foreign investors may also be deterred by the difficulties of doing business with China.
Ever-changing policies, government inefficiency and a dearth of qualified staff are among some of the problems plaguing foreign investors.
